extracted.intended_audience: researchers and instructors in undergraduate mathematics education (especially those teaching proof-based/advanced undergraduate courses)
extracted.subtask_description: A method and associated coding/scoring guidance for analyzing the enacted example space in advanced undergraduate/proof-based mathematics courses, plus a classroom problem-solving scoring guide used in an algebra course study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example neighborhood
rubrics_metrics.description: The entire collection of examples (including pertinent non-examples) that the students are exposed to during the course of their studies of a particular construct (e.g., the sequence of examples given to support the definition of a concept).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the example neighborhood on four levels: (1) what is the first example given, (2) what examples are near the concept temporally, (3) what is the range of permissible variation that students experience, and (4) what variation constraint do students experience. Pay special attention to the first few examples (they often shape students' concept images). Describe how examples vary from one to the next and whether they vary along more than one dimension at a time. Include non-examples and note how they limit the concept. Present as a narrative describing each example and its temporal position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how examples are created and what tools/methods for creating additional examples students are exposed to (the means of construction that allow students to populate the example space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe methods for constructing examples observed or taught (including instructor-provided construction methods and tasks that require students to construct examples). Use this to predict the tools students have to create novel examples. Consider instructor strategies ranging from providing many examples but few construction tools to providing few examples but rich construction methods; neither extreme is held normative but both impact students' ability to develop their own example spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the function(s) an example serves in classroom discourse, in two senses: which examples are called upon most often (frequency/readiness), and the mathematical intent of the example (what it was being used to do).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record frequency of use (frequently used examples may obtain 'ready access' status/evoked concept image). Classify the mathematical intent: exemplifying a definition, creating or refining a definition, articulating or exploring a conjecture, illustrating a proof, providing counterexamples/non-examples, or offering clues to proofs. Use classroom-context notes to describe subsequent uses of the example (e.g., did it inform student work or later instruction?).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-filter method (enacted example space assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedure using three filters — (1) example neighborhood, (2) example construction, and (3) function of the example — to describe and analyze the enacted example space and thereby assess the mathematical quality of instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply each filter separately and then read them together to analyze the example space. The three rounds of assessment together contribute to judgments about instructional quality at the advanced undergraduate level. Use empirical data (video, handouts, homework, exams) to populate each filter and justify analyses with examples from the enacted curriculum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example-neighborhood organization criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific evaluative attention points within the neighborhood: identification of the first example, temporal proximity of examples, range of permissible variation, and variation constraints experienced by students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Dienes' recommendation: students should encounter sets of examples that are narrowly constructed (vary along a limited number of dimensions) so they can discern structural vs. variable aspects. Early examples should be carefully chosen to avoid creating misleading concept images; early examples varying along too many dimensions may reduce learning value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example log coding scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-column coding/logging format to record each example or non-example observed in class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Columns: (1) list the example/non-example; (2) number of class meetings since the formal definition (to fix temporal position in example neighborhood); (3) qualities/properties of the example or missing properties for non-examples (to describe range of permissible variation); (4) manner in which the example was made part of classroom discourse and how it was used (to capture function). Use coded logs to summarize the enacted example neighborhood, constructed examples, and example functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of variation constraints (Dienes/variation theory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion that students should experience example sets that vary along constrained dimensions in order to 'locate dimensions of possible variation' and discern what aspects are structural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether examples are presented in narrowly constructed sets (each set varying along a limited number of dimensions) and whether multiple sets cover different dimensions. Note when early examples produce restrictive concept images or when collections fail to support student construction of critical aspects of the concept. Explicitly evaluate the range of permissible variation (e.g., cardinality, commutativity, finiteness) presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner-generated examples as formative assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice and criterion of asking students to construct examples as a diagnostic/formative tool to evaluate their understanding of definitions and concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether instruction includes tasks requiring student-generated examples, and use those student examples to diagnose misconceptions or problematic aspects of student understanding. Record how instructors respond to learner-generated examples and whether such examples are used to guide subsequent instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on inferring student engagement from observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Caveat/criterion about what inferences about student engagement can reasonably be made from classroom observation and enacted-curriculum artifacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make strong low-inference judgments about students' depth of engagement from observation alone. Distinguish suggested vs. required homework, note observed active engagement when present, but otherwise make few claims about out-of-class engagement. Acknowledge measurement difficulties (e.g., silent attention in lecture vs. unmonitored group work).

rubrics_metrics.name: MA 098/110 Scoring Guide — Conceptual Understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubric dimension: 'Interpreting the concepts of the task and translating them into mathematics' with point levels (2, 1, 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 2: The translation of the task into adequate mathematical concepts using relevant information is completed. Level 1: The translation of the major concepts of the task is partially completed and/or partially displayed. Level 0: Does not achieve minimal requirements for 1 point. (Loosely adapted from Oregon Dept. of Education statewide assessments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: MA 098/110 Scoring Guide — Evidence of Problem Solving
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubric dimension: 'Choosing strategies that can work, and then carrying out the strategies chosen' with point levels (2, 1, 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 2: Strategy that can work is chosen and carried out effectively. Level 1: Strategy partially completed and/or partially displayed. Level 0: Does not achieve minimal requirements for 1 point. Use this to assess selection and execution of problem-solving approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: MA 098/110 Scoring Guide — Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubric dimension: 'Using pictures, symbols, and/or vocabulary to convey the path to the identified solution' with point levels (2, 1, 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 2: Pictures, models, diagrams, symbols, and/or words used to solve the task are complete and explanation is clear and complete. Level 1: Representations/explanations are partially complete and/or partially developed with gaps that have to be inferred. Level 0: Does not achieve minimal requirements for 1 point.

rubrics_metrics.name: MA 098/110 Scoring Guide — Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Rubric dimension: 'Providing a complete and accurate solution appropriate for the given problem' with point levels (2, 1, 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level 2: Solution is correct and complete with no errors. Level 1: Solution is appropriate and demonstrates understanding, but is either not quite complete or contains minor errors. Level 0: Does not achieve minimal requirements for 1 point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of rubric-scored pre/post test (Part 1) to capture communication/problem-solving gains
rubrics_metrics.description: Design principle: use a rubric-scored open-response (Part 1) pre/post test to measure improvements in students' ability to express mathematical thinking (distinct from objective Part 2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that rubric-scored open responses can capture gains in problem solving and communication even when objective measures (multiple-choice) do not change. Ensure rubrics target conceptual understanding, problem-solving evidence, explanation, and accuracy (as in MA 098/110 scoring guide).
